content: Wasting, in medical terminology, refers to the progressive loss of muscle and fat tissue caused by a debilitating disease. This condition is sometimes referred to as acute malnutrition because it is typically associated with a short duration, unlike stunting, which is considered a manifestation of chronic malnutrition. Wasting can result from various factors, including insufficient food intake (e.g., due to famine), nutrient losses caused by infections, or a combination of low dietary intake and increased nutrient losses. Infections commonly associated with wasting include tuberculosis, chronic diarrhea, and AIDS. The underlying mechanism may involve the action of cachectin, also known as tumor necrosis factor (TNF), a cytokine secreted by macrophages that plays a role in inflammation and tissue breakdown. In some cases, caregivers or healthcare providers may inadvertently contribute to wasting by imposing overly restrictive diets on patients. However, voluntary weight loss and eating disorders are not considered causes of wasting. Classification of Wasting: In Children: Wasting in children is assessed using the weight-for-height (WFH) index. For infants under 24 months of age, recumbent (supine) length is used to calculate WFH as a percentage of the median reference value. A WFH below 80% of the median (approximately equivalent to a -2 Z-score) is often used as a cutoff point to define wasting. In Adults: Wasting in adults is typically evaluated using the Body Mass Index (BMI), which is calculated as weight (in kilograms) divided by height squared (in meters). A BMI below 18.5 kg/m² is generally considered indicative of wasting. Additionally, unintentional weight loss is another criterion; for example, at Tufts University, an unintentional loss of 6% or more of body weight within six months is regarded as wasting.
